554.title: Blessed is the one who spoke
554.hook: the opening blessing praises the one who spoke and the world came to be
554.howItsDone: Baruch She'amar opens the verses of song in the morning service; in many communities people stand for it, and those wearing a tallit hold the two front fringes and kiss them at the closing blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pesukei d'Zimra, the verses of song that warm the heart. Your line was warm up the heart. What did you warm up for? Today, the blessing that opens the songs. Day five hundred fifty-four.

Words make things happen. A judge says guilty, and a life changes. Two people say I do, and they're married. A friend says I'm sorry, and something heals. Most of the time, though, our words are cheap. We say we'll call and don't. We say five minutes and mean twenty. Now imagine a speaker whose every word becomes real, at once, with no gap at all. In many synagogues the room stands up for the blessing that praises exactly that.
screen: `WORDS MAKE THINGS HAPPEN.` → `MOSTLY, OUR WORDS ARE CHEAP.` → `A SPEAKER WITH NO GAP.`

segments.voice: It begins: baruch she'amar v'hayah ha'olam, blessed is the one who spoke, and the world came to be. It points back to the first page of the Torah. In the old Jewish translation: "And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light." No tools, no raw materials in the story. Just speech, and then the world. Then the blessing builds, one short line after another, each starting with the same word, baruch, blessed. Blessed is the one who makes creation. Blessed is the one who says and does. Who decrees and fulfills. Who has mercy on the earth. Who has mercy on the creatures. Who rewards those who revere him. Who lives forever. Who redeems and rescues. Line after line, like a drumbeat. Notice two lines in the middle: mercy on the earth, and mercy on the creatures. The world isn't only spoken into being and left; the same voice keeps caring for it. Customs gather around this blessing. Many people stand. Many who wear a prayer shawl hold its two front fringes during the blessing and kiss them at the end. A late tradition says the text came down from heaven on a written note, and that its words number eighty-seven. Whatever its history, it opens the songs with the most basic praise there is: the world exists because someone spoke, and kept their word.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SPOKE, AND THE WORLD WAS.` · `BARUCH, BARUCH, LIKE A DRUMBEAT.` · `MERCY ON THE EARTH AND CREATURES.` · `STAND, HOLD THE FRINGES, KISS.` · then, large: `BLESSED WHO SPOKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it before something new. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you're about to start: a project, a meal, a conversation, a week. Picture its first moment. Before that moment, put a pause. If you pray, you can say the opening words, baruch she'amar v'hayah ha'olam, blessed is the one who spoke and the world came to be. If not, just notice that this new thing also begins with words. Then think of one promise you've made lately, and decide to keep it. The bell holds the time.
Baruch She'amar. Blessed is the one who spoke: the blessing that opens the verses of song.
Your line: blessed who spoke. Today, make your words a little less cheap: say only what you'll do, and do what you said. Day five hundred fifty-four.

555.title: Give thanks (1 Chronicles 16:8)
555.hook: "O give thanks unto the LORD, call upon His name", David's song for the ark
555.howItsDone: Hodu, from 1 Chronicles 16, is said each morning in the verses of song: after Baruch She'amar in the Ashkenazi rite, and before it in many Sephardi rites.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baruch She'amar, blessed is the one who spoke. Your line was blessed who spoke. Did you keep the promise you picked? Today, the first song after that blessing. Day five hundred fifty-five.

The ark of the covenant, the gold-covered chest that held the tablets, has been away for years: captured in battle, sent back, kept for months in one family's house. Now, at last, King David brings it up to Jerusalem. There's music, shouting, the sound of horns. David himself dances. And when the ark is set down in the tent he's pitched for it, the story says he does something before anything else. He puts singers in place. And he hands them a song that begins with two words, in Hebrew, hodu ladonai.
screen: `THE ARK COMES HOME.` → `DAVID DANCES.` → `FIRST, HE APPOINTS SINGERS.`

segments.voice: The Book of Chronicles gives the song in full. In the old Jewish translation it opens: "O give thanks unto the LORD, call upon His name; make known His doings among the peoples." And near its end comes a line that runs all through Jewish prayer: "O give thanks unto the LORD; for He is good; for His mercy endureth for ever." Look closely and the song is a weave. Its opening lines also appear in Psalm one hundred five, its middle in Psalm ninety-six, its close in Psalm one hundred six. Chronicles stitches them together for one great day. In the Ashkenazi prayer book, the passage comes right after Baruch She'amar; in many Sephardi prayer books, just before it. Either way, a morning of song begins where David began: with thanks. Notice the second half of that first verse. Make known his doings among the peoples. Thanks here isn't only a private feeling. It's said out loud, so others hear the story. And the Hebrew word itself, hodu, give thanks, carries an echo. In Genesis, when Leah names her fourth son, she says: this time I will praise the LORD. His name is Judah, Yehudah, built from that same root. The tribe of Judah, and centuries later the word Jew, trace back to that name. So a word for giving thanks sits close to the name the people carry.
screen: `DAVID BRINGS THE ARK HOME.` · `HODU: O GIVE THANKS.` · `A WEAVE OF THREE PSALMS.` · `JUDAH: THIS TIME I WILL PRAISE.` · then, large: `GIVE THANKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone where others can hear. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person who did something good for you lately and didn't get much credit. A coworker who covered for you. A neighbor. A sibling. Picture what they did, in detail. Then shape one sentence of thanks you could say in front of others: in a group chat, at dinner, in a meeting. Make it specific. Not thanks for everything, but thanks for this. If you pray, you can say hodu ladonai, give thanks to the LORD. The bell holds the time.
Give thanks. Hodu: David's song for the ark, sung each morning near the start of the verses of song.
Your line: give thanks. Today, say your sentence of thanks out loud, where others can hear it. Day five hundred fifty-five.

556.title: Serve with gladness (Psalm 100)
556.hook: a thanksgiving psalm said on weekdays: "Serve the LORD with gladness"
556.howItsDone: In the Ashkenazi rite, Psalm 100 is said in the weekday verses of song, often while standing and with joy, and is left out on Shabbat, festivals, the eve of Passover, the intermediate days of Passover and the eve of Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hodu, David's song for the ark. Your line was give thanks. Who heard you thank someone out loud? Today, a short psalm that's skipped on the holiest days. Day five hundred fifty-six.

There are two ways to wash the dishes. One with a sigh, scraping plates and counting the minutes. One with music on, maybe humming, the warm water on your hands. Same dishes. Same time. A completely different hour of your life. The difference isn't the task. It's the gladness you bring to it. Among the verses of song is a psalm only five verses long, and in its second line it puts those two words side by side, serve and gladness, as if they belong together.
screen: `TWO WAYS TO WASH THE DISHES.` → `SAME TASK, DIFFERENT HOUR.` → `SERVE, AND GLADNESS.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred has a heading, in the old Jewish translation: "A Psalm of thanksgiving." In Hebrew, mizmor l'todah. A todah was a particular offering in the Temple, the thanksgiving offering, brought by someone who'd come through danger: a journey, an illness, a prison. Then the psalm: "Shout unto the LORD, all the earth. Serve the LORD with gladness; come before His presence with singing." The Hebrew for serve, avdu, comes from avodah, a word that means both work and worship. The same word for hauling stones and for prayer. The psalm says: do it with simchah, with joy. Now the surprising part. In the Ashkenazi custom, this psalm is said on weekdays but skipped on Shabbat and festivals. Why? Because the thanksgiving offering, a personal, voluntary gift, wasn't brought on those days. It's skipped, too, before Passover and through the festival, because the thanksgiving offering included loaves of leavened bread. The prayer book remembers the Temple calendar even here. And a midrash says something lovely about it. In the time to come, it says, all the offerings will cease except the thanksgiving offering. All prayers will cease except the prayer of thanks. Some teachers say that's why this psalm should be said with real joy, even sung. Of everything in the service, thanks is the part meant to last.
screen: `MIZMOR L'TODAH: A PSALM OF THANKS.` · `AVODAH: WORK AND WORSHIP.` · `SKIPPED ON SHABBAT AND FESTIVALS.` · `ONLY THANKS WILL LAST.` · then, large: `SERVE WITH GLADNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one task gladly. Settle, and breathe. Pick one chore waiting for you today: dishes, email, laundry, the commute. Picture doing it the sighing way, and notice how it feels in your chest. Then picture it again: same task, but slower, with a song, with attention to the warm water or the sunlight through the bus window. Notice what changes. If you pray, you can say ivdu et Hashem b'simchah, serve the LORD with gladness. The bell holds the time.
Serve with gladness. From Psalm one hundred, the psalm of thanksgiving, said on weekdays in the verses of song.
Your line: serve with gladness. Today, do the chore you picked the glad way, and notice whether the hour feels different. Day five hundred fifty-six.

557.title: The missing letter (Berakhot 4b)
557.hook: Psalm 145 runs through the alphabet but skips nun, the teachers say to avoid a verse about falling
557.howItsDone: Ashrei, built around Psalm 145, is said twice in the morning service and once in the afternoon service; in the morning it is the center of the verses of song.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm one hundred, the psalm of thanksgiving. Your line was serve with gladness. Did the chore feel different done gladly? Today, the psalm said three times a day, and the letter it leaves out. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

Psalm one hundred forty-five is an acrostic. Each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet: alef, bet, gimel, and on down the line. It's built to be memorized; children learn it young, and many Jews say it three times every day, twice in the morning and once in the afternoon. It's the heart of the prayer called Ashrei. But count the verses and something's off. There are twenty-two letters in the alphabet. Psalm one hundred forty-five has twenty-one verses. One letter, right in the middle, is missing.
screen: `AN ALPHABET PSALM.` → `SAID THREE TIMES A DAY.` → `ONE LETTER IS MISSING.`

segments.voice: The missing letter is nun, the letter for the sound N. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, asks why. Rabbi Yochanan answers: because a terrible verse begins with nun. In the prophet Amos: fallen is the maiden Israel, she shall rise no more. Nafelah, fallen, starts with nun. So the psalmist, the teachers say, left the letter out rather than bring that word anywhere near a song of praise. Then another rabbi, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, adds the beautiful part. Even so, he says, David came back and caught them. Look at the very next verse, the one beginning with samech, the letter after nun. In the old Jewish translation: "The LORD upholdeth all that fall, and raiseth up all those that are bowed down." The word fall is right there. Not as a sentence, but as something caught. The fall is acknowledged, then immediately held. Now, what does the scholar hear? Among the Dead Sea Scrolls is a copy of this psalm that does have a nun verse: God is faithful in his words, and gracious in all his deeds. The ancient Greek translation has one too. So some scholars think a nun line once existed and dropped out of the traditional Hebrew text. The Talmud's reading doesn't depend on that question. It's a teaching about how to sing: you can leave a painful word unsaid, and still, in the next breath, say that the fallen are lifted.
screen: `NUN IS MISSING.` · `FALLEN, SHE SHALL RISE NO MORE.` · `THE NEXT VERSE CATCHES THEM.` · `A NUN LINE IN THE DEAD SEA SCROLLS.` · then, large: `THE MISSING LETTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what was left out kindly. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last few weeks for a moment when someone could have said the hard thing, and didn't. A friend who didn't mention your mistake. A parent who let a bad grade go. Someone who changed the subject to spare you. Picture the word they didn't say. Then picture what they did instead: a hand on your shoulder, a joke, a lift home. That's the samech after the missing nun. The bell holds the time.
The missing letter. Nun, left out of Psalm one hundred forty-five, the Talmud says, so the song never speaks of falling without catching.
Your line: the missing letter. Today, leave one hard word unsaid on purpose, and say something that lifts instead. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

558.title: Five hallelujahs (Psalms 146–150)
558.hook: the last five psalms, each beginning and ending with praise
558.howItsDone: Psalms 146–150 are said every morning in the verses of song, right after Ashrei, with the last verse of Psalm 150 repeated; in many synagogues they are chanted quickly together, and the final verses are sung aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the missing letter in Psalm one hundred forty-five. Your line was the missing letter. What hard word did you leave unsaid? Today, the five psalms that come right after it. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

Hallelujah. It might be the one Hebrew word nearly everyone on earth knows. People shout it in gospel choirs, sing it in Handel's Messiah, mutter it when the bus finally comes. It turns up in songs and slogans and greeting cards. Most people who say it have no idea it's Hebrew, or that it's an instruction. And in the Jewish morning service, right after Ashrei, it comes ten times in a row, like bookends: at the start and the end of the last five psalms in the Bible.
screen: `A WORD EVERYONE KNOWS.` → `IT'S HEBREW, AND AN INSTRUCTION.` → `TEN TIMES, LIKE BOOKENDS.`

segments.voice: Hallelu means praise, said to a group: all of you, praise. Yah is a short form of God's name. So hallelujah is a call: everyone, praise God. Psalms one hundred forty-six through one hundred fifty each open with it and each close with it. Five psalms, ten hallelujahs. Listen to how the praise widens. The first of the five praises God for the people at the bottom: the prisoner, the blind, the stranger, the orphan, the widow. The second, in the old Jewish translation, says God is the one "Who healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds," and in the same breath counts the stars and calls each one by name. The third calls on everything to praise: sun and moon, sea creatures, fire and hail, kings and children, old and young. The fourth asks for a new song. And the last one is almost all music: the horn, the harp, the drum, dancing, strings, pipes, cymbals, loud cymbals. Then the final line of the whole Book of Psalms: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Hallelujah." The prayer book says that last line twice. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, records Rabbi Yose's wish to be among those who finish the praise every day, and it's understood to mean these psalms. So the Book of Psalms, with all its grief and pleading, ends here: not with an answer, but with everything that breathes, praising.
screen: `HALLELU-YAH: ALL OF YOU, PRAISE GOD.` · `THE PRISONER, THE STRANGER, THE WIDOW.` · `HEALS HEARTS, COUNTS STARS.` · `EVERY THING THAT HATH BREATH.` · then, large: `HALLELUJAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one of them. Settle, and breathe. If you have a Bible or a prayer book nearby, open to Psalm one hundred fifty; it's only six verses. Read it slowly, out loud if you can. If you don't have it, go back to the last line you heard: let every thing that hath breath. Breathe in, and notice your own breath counts. Then think of three other things that breathe near you: a person, a pet, a tree outside. If you pray, end with hallelujah. The bell holds the time.
Five hallelujahs. Psalms one hundred forty-six to one hundred fifty, each opening and closing with hallelujah: all of you, praise God.
Your line: hallelujah. Today, when you hear the word, in a song, on a sign, from a friend, remember it's a call to everyone that breathes. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

559.title: The sea every morning (Exodus 15)
559.hook: the verses of song end with the Song of the Sea, sung daily
559.howItsDone: The Song of the Sea (Exodus 14:30–15:18) is said each morning near the end of the verses of song, often standing, and it is read from the Torah on the seventh day of Passover and on Shabbat Shirah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five hallelujahs that close the Book of Psalms. Your line was hallelujah. Where did you hear the word? Today, the song the verses of song build toward. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

A people who were slaves the week before are standing on the far shore of a sea. Behind them, the water has closed. In front of them, the desert, and no idea what comes next. They crossed on dry ground, and now they're exhausted, terrified and alive. And they sing. Moses sings, and the people sing with him, and Miriam takes a drum and the women dance. Many scholars count it among the oldest poems in the Bible. And every morning, at the very end of the verses of song, Jews who pray the full service sing it again, as if they'd just stepped out onto that shore.
screen: `SLAVES LAST WEEK.` → `ALIVE ON THE FAR SHORE.` → `THEY SING.`

segments.voice: It's called Shirat HaYam, the Song of the Sea, from Exodus fifteen. In the old Jewish translation it begins: "I will sing unto the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea." Then, a line that turns up all over Jewish prayer: "The LORD is my strength and song." Even the way it's written is different. In a Torah scroll, this song isn't laid out in plain columns. The Talmud describes it as half bricks over whole bricks: short lines and gaps staggered like a wall, so you can spot it from across the room. The opening words are az yashir, then sang Moses. But the Hebrew verb can also be read as will sing, and the Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin, hears in that a hint that the song isn't over, that it will be sung again in a world to come. Some commentators say to say it each morning with joy, as if you yourself had crossed that day. And there's a famous counterweight. The Talmud tells that when the Egyptians were drowning, the angels wanted to sing too, and God stopped them: the work of my hands is drowning in the sea, and you would sing? Israel's song of rescue is kept, every morning. But the tradition remembers that the rescue had a cost, and that God grieves for every creature.
screen: `SHIRAT HAYAM: THE SONG OF THE SEA.` · `WRITTEN LIKE A WALL OF BRICKS.` · `AZ YASHIR: SANG, OR WILL SING.` · `MY HANDIWORK IS DROWNING.` · then, large: `THE SEA SONG EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing one line aloud. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time you came through something: an illness, a move, a loss, a terrible year. Picture yourself on the far shore of it. Then sing one line, any line that feels like that moment. If you know it, the Hebrew ozi v'zimrat Yah, the LORD is my strength and song. If not, a song you love. Out loud, even softly, even off-key. Then let it go quiet, and remember someone who didn't make it through with you. The bell holds the time.
The sea every morning. Shirat HaYam, the Song of the Sea, sung daily at the end of the verses of song.
Your line: the sea song every day. Today, remember once that you are on the far shore of something, and hum your line. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

560.title: Yishtabach
560.hook: the closing blessing of the verses of song
560.howItsDone: Yishtabach closes the verses of song every morning, often said standing; it is followed by half Kaddish and the call to prayer, Barchu, which opens the Shema and its blessings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Song of the Sea, sung every morning. Your line was the sea song every day. What far shore did you remember? Today, the last word of the verses of song, and the end of this week. Day five hundred sixty.

Every good piece of music knows how to end. The last chord of a symphony. The final chorus that everyone sings. Even a playlist has a last song you pick on purpose. Endings tell you what the whole thing was about. The verses of song have been building for a while now: the blessing for the one who spoke, David's thanks, the alphabet psalm, five hallelujahs, the sea. Then they close with a single paragraph. It doesn't add a new idea. It gathers up every word for praise it can find and stacks them, like a final chord.
screen: `ENDINGS SAY WHAT IT WAS ABOUT.` → `THE SONGS HAVE BEEN BUILDING.` → `A FINAL CHORD.`

segments.voice: It's called Yishtabach, from its first word: yishtabach shimcha la'ad malkeinu, may your name be praised forever, our king. Then the stack. To you belong song and praise, hallel and hymn, strength and dominion, victory, greatness and might, praise and glory, holiness and sovereignty, blessings and thanksgivings. Count them and you get fifteen. Commentators have connected that number to the fifteen Songs of Ascents in the Psalms, and to the fifteen steps in the Temple where, the Mishnah says, the Levites stood and sang. Notice something about the form. Most blessings start with baruch, blessed. Yishtabach doesn't. That's because it isn't a separate blessing. It's the closing half of Baruch She'amar, the blessing that opened the verses of song. The two are bookends around everything in between, and many communities avoid talking between them. Look at the opening words in Hebrew, too. The first letters of shimcha, la'ad, malkeinu and ha'el spell Shlomo, Solomon, and a tradition credits him with the prayer. That may be a later reading, but it shows how closely people have looked at every word. And the very last phrase is lovely. It calls God habocher b'shirei zimrah: the one who chooses songs of praise. Not the one who demands them. The one who chooses them. As if, out of everything in the world, the songs people sing are something God picks out and wants.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end one task with praise. Settle, and breathe. Think of the last thing you finished today: a meal, a shift, a phone call, this lesson. Before moving on, give it an ending. Name one good thing in it. Then another. Stack them, the way Yishtabach stacks its words: it was warm, it was useful, someone laughed, it's done. If you pray, you can close with the words yishtabach shimcha la'ad, may your name be praised forever. The bell holds the time.
Yishtabach. May it be praised: the blessing that closes the verses of song with fifteen words of praise.

Your line: praised forever. A week of the verses of song: the one who spoke, give thanks, gladness, the missing letter, five hallelujahs, the sea, and Yishtabach. Today, end your workday with three good things, stacked. Day five hundred sixty.
